# `silk/bench/suite`

<!-- Generated by silk doc-reference. Do not edit by hand. -->

Describes what a benchmark run compares: suites, their implementations, the programs to
time, and where the reports go.

## When to use
Build a [`Suite`](#Suite) in a project's `tasks.silk` and give it to `silk.bench.bench.Bench.perform`. A
suite compares implementations of one piece of work: a Silk program and the same program in
another language, two versions of one program, or one program with different options.

## Details
A command suite, from [`Suite.command`](#Suite.impl.command), times whole processes: any program in any language
is an implementation, with nothing to adopt. An [`Implementation`](#Implementation) is one program with its
arguments. A [`Call`](#Call) is a program a hook runs without timing it: [`Suite.setup`](#Suite.impl.setup) and
[`Suite.cleanup`](#Suite.impl.cleanup) run once around the suite, and [`Implementation.prepare`](#Implementation.impl.prepare) and
[`Implementation.conclude`](#Implementation.impl.conclude) run around every timed run.

Every path is a `silk.build.step.Deferred<Path>` from the build system, resolved when the
task runs: a package file from `Deferred<Path>.source`, a host path from
`Deferred<Path>.external`, or the output of a build step, such as a compilation's
`artifact()` or a `Run` step that builds a program in another language. The steps a suite's
paths come from run before anything is timed, with the build system's cache, so a second run
rebuilds nothing that did not change.

A program that measures itself says so with [`Implementation.resultLines`](#Implementation.impl.resultLines): the suite then
reads the result lines the program prints, one sample a line, and reports what the lines
say in their own unit, such as `ns/op` or `req/s`. A load generator, a server benchmark, or
a loop that times one function inside a larger program reports this way.
[`Implementation.googleBenchmark`](#Implementation.impl.googleBenchmark) and [`Implementation.criterion`](#Implementation.impl.criterion) say the same of a program
that prints the table of Google Benchmark or the lines of a Rust benchmark.

A program that holds several benchmarks and can run each on request says so with
[`Implementation.driven`](#Implementation.impl.driven): the suite keeps it alive, decides how many iterations a sample
takes, and takes the samples of the implementations in turns.

[`Suite.parameter`](#Suite.impl.parameter) runs the suite once for each value: `{name}` in an argument is replaced
by the value, and each combination of values is its own benchmark, named
`suite/name=value`. [`Suite.cpus`](#Suite.impl.cpus) does the same for the number of processors a program may
run on, as the parameter `cpus`.

[`Suite.view`](#Suite.impl.view) declares how the reports show the results, as a `silk.bench.view.View`: a
line against a parameter, every sample, a comparison against another implementation.

[`Suite.output`](#Suite.impl.output) declares where a report goes: an [`Output`](#Output) is a [`Format`](#Format) and a place,
standard output or a file. A suite without outputs prints the terminal table.

## Examples
```silk,ignore
import silk.bench.suite { Format, Implementation, Output, Suite }
import silk.build.graph { BuildError, Compilation, Options }
import silk.build.step { Deferred }
import silk.mem.allocator { Allocator }
import silk.system.filesystem { FileSystem, Path }
import silk.system.host_input { HostInput }

// Compares this package's program with a Rust build of the same work, on two inputs.
effect fn jsonParse(options: &Options) -> Suite
  ! BuildError
  ? &mut Allocator | &mut FileSystem | &mut HostInput {
  let compilation = run Compilation.fromPackage(options)
  let mut silk = Implementation.program(run compilation.artifact())
  run silk.path(run Deferred<Path>.source("data/{file}.json"))

  let mut rust = Implementation.program(run Deferred<Path>.source("rust/target/release/parse"))
  run rust.path(run Deferred<Path>.source("data/{file}.json"))

  let mut suite = run Suite.command("json-parse")
  run suite.implementation("silk", move silk)
  run suite.implementation("rust", move rust)
  run suite.reference("rust")
  run suite.parameter("file", &["twitter", "canada"])
  run suite.output(Output.stdout(Format.Terminal))
  run suite.output(Output.file(run Deferred<Path>.source("build/bench/json.html"), Format.Html))
  return move suite
}
```

Import as `Suite` with `import silk.bench.suite { Suite }`.

<a id="Implementation.impl.resultLines"></a>

### Method `resultLines`

```silk
pub fn resultLines(self: &mut Self) -> ()
```

Says that the program prints result lines, as `silk.bench.lines` describes them, and that
the suite measures what those lines report, not the time of the process.

#### Details
Each line is one sample of the benchmark its name gives, so one run of the program may
report many benchmarks and many samples of each. The program writes the lines to standard
output, or to the file the environment variable `BENCH_OUT` names, which the suite sets
for every timed run. Lines that are not result lines are ignored.

The suite reads four configuration keys. `check:` says what the program computed, such
as a checksum or a count: implementations whose checks differ for one benchmark are not
compared, and the task fails. `revision:` is recorded as the implementation's revision
when the suite gives none. `note:` is added to the notes of the run.
`view:` suggests a view, as `silk.bench.view.View.parse` reads it, which the reports show
when the suite declares none.

<a id="Implementation.impl.googleBenchmark"></a>

### Method `googleBenchmark`

```silk
pub fn googleBenchmark(self: &mut Self) -> ()
```

Says that the program is a Google Benchmark program, and that the suite measures what its
console table reports, as [`Implementation.resultLines`](#Implementation.impl.resultLines) does for result lines.

#### Details
Each row of the table is one sample: its `Time` column is reported as `ns/op` and its
`CPU` column as `cpu-ns/op`. The rows Google Benchmark adds for repetitions are left out.
`silk.bench.lines.Lines.fromGoogleBenchmark` does the reading. The program must print the
table to standard output, which is what it does without `--benchmark_format`.

<a id="Implementation.impl.criterion"></a>

### Method `criterion`

```silk
pub fn criterion(self: &mut Self) -> ()
```

Says that the program is a Rust benchmark, run by Criterion or by the built-in harness,
and that the suite measures what it reports, as [`Implementation.resultLines`](#Implementation.impl.resultLines) does for
result lines.

#### Details
Each `name  time:   [low estimate high]` line of Criterion is one sample, the estimate in
the middle, and so is each `test name ... bench: 1,240 ns/iter (+/- 12)` line. Both are
reported as `ns/op`. `silk.bench.lines.Lines.fromCriterion` does the reading. The program
must print to standard output, as `cargo bench` does.

<a id="Implementation.impl.driven"></a>

### Method `driven`

```silk
pub fn driven(self: &mut Self) -> ()
```

Says that the program is a harness the task drives, as `silk.bench.transport` describes:
the task starts it with `BENCH_DRIVE=1`, asks it for its benchmarks, and asks for one
sample at a time over its standard input and output.

#### Details
The task finds how many iterations of each benchmark take the suite's sample time, and
then, in each round, takes one sample of each benchmark from every implementation, in a
random order. The programs stay alive between samples, and each is started again a few
times over a run, so that one unlucky start does not color every sample. The report is in
the unit of the harness, `ns/op`.

A Silk program answers with `silk.bench.harness.Harness`. A program in another language
reads the commands from its standard input and prints result lines, which takes a loop of
a few dozen lines.

```silk
    ! OutOfMemoryError
    ? &mut Allocator
```

Names the implementation the others are compared to. Without it, the first one added is

<a id="Suite.impl.parameter"></a>

### Method `parameter`

```silk
pub effect fn parameter(self: &mut Self, name: string, values: &[string]) -> ()
    ! OutOfMemoryError
    ? &mut Allocator
```

Adds the parameter `name` with `values`. The suite runs once for each value, and once for
each combination when it has several parameters.

<a id="Suite.impl.cpus"></a>

### Method `cpus`

```silk
pub effect fn cpus(self: &mut Self, counts: &[u32]) -> ()
    ! OutOfMemoryError
    ? &mut Allocator
```

Runs the suite once for each of `counts`, with every program limited to that many
processors, as the parameter `cpus`. The limit is an affinity mask over the first
processors the task may use.

#### Gotchas
Only Linux can limit processors. On another system, a suite with this setting fails
before anything is timed.

<a id="Suite.impl.runs"></a>

### Method `runs`

```silk
pub fn runs(self: &mut Self, count: u64) -> ()
```

Sets the number of measured rounds. Every implementation runs once in each round, in a
random order. The default is 10. `--runs` on the command line wins.

<a id="Suite.impl.warmup"></a>

### Method `warmup`

```silk
pub fn warmup(self: &mut Self, count: u64) -> ()
```

Sets the number of warm-up rounds, which fill caches before the measured rounds and are
in no statistic. The default is 1. `--warmup` on the command line wins.

<a id="Suite.impl.sample"></a>

### Method `sample`

```silk
pub fn sample(self: &mut Self, milliseconds: u64) -> ()
```

Sets how long one sample of a driven implementation should take, in milliseconds: the
task asks for as many iterations as fill that time. The default is 50.

### Method `setup`

```silk
pub effect fn setup(self: &mut Self, call: Call) -> ()
    ! OutOfMemoryError
    ? &mut Allocator
```

Adds a call that runs once before anything is timed. A call that fails stops the run.

```silk
    ! OutOfMemoryError
```


Adds a report. A suite with at least one output prints nothing else: add
`Output.stdout(Format.Terminal)` to keep the table.

<a id="Suite.impl.view"></a>

### Method `view`

```silk
pub effect fn view(self: &mut Self, view: View) -> ()
    ! OutOfMemoryError
    ? &mut Allocator
```

Adds a view: one more way the reports show the results. A suite with at least one view
gets no other: without any, a report picks views by the shape of the results.
